claim: Mycofactocin is a redox cofactor essential for the alcohol metabolism of mycobacteria.
source: Mycofactocin is a redox cofactor essential for the alcohol metabolism of mycobacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational claim about mycofactocin's role.

claim: MftG encodes an oxidoreductase of the glucose-methanol-choline superfamily.
source: the gene mftG, which encodes an oxidoreductase of the glucose-methanol-choline superfamily, remained functionally uncharacterized.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the protein family classification of MftG.

claim: MftG enzymes are almost exclusively found in genomes containing mycofactocin biosynthetic genes.
source: MftG enzymes are almost exclusively found in genomes containing mycofactocin biosynthetic genes and are present in 75% of organisms harboring these genes.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a finding from bioinformatics analysis.

claim: MftG enzymes are present in 75% of organisms harboring mycofactocin biosynthetic genes.
source: MftG enzymes are almost exclusively found in genomes containing mycofactocin biosynthetic genes and are present in 75% of organisms harboring these genes.
evidence: The abstract provides a specific percentage from co-occurrence analysis.

claim: Gene deletion of mftG in Mycolicibacterium smegmatis demonstrated a growth defect on ethanol as a carbon source.
source: Gene deletion experiments in Mycolicibacterium smegmatis demonstrated a growth defect of the ∆mftG mutant on ethanol as a carbon source, accompanied by an arrest of cell division reminiscent of mild starvation.
evidence: The abstract describes experimental results from gene deletion studies.

claim: The ∆mftG mutant exhibited an arrest of cell division reminiscent of mild starvation.
source: Gene deletion experiments in Mycolicibacterium smegmatis demonstrated a growth defect of the ∆mftG mutant on ethanol as a carbon source, accompanied by an arrest of cell division reminiscent of mild starvation.
evidence: The abstract describes phenotypic observations from the mutant.

claim: Investigation of carbon and cofactor metabolism implied a defect in mycofactocin reoxidation in the ∆mftG mutant.
source: Investigation of carbon and cofactor metabolism implied a defect in mycofactocin reoxidation.
evidence: The abstract states this as an interpretation of metabolic studies.

claim: Cell-free enzyme assays indicated that MftG acts as a mycofactocin dehydrogenase.
source: Cell-free enzyme assays and respirometry using isolated cell membranes indicated that MftG acts as a mycofactocin dehydrogenase shuttling electrons toward the respiratory chain.
evidence: The abstract describes results from in vitro enzyme assays.

claim: Respirometry using isolated cell membranes indicated that MftG shuttles electrons toward the respiratory chain.
source: Cell-free enzyme assays and respirometry using isolated cell membranes indicated that MftG acts as a mycofactocin dehydrogenase shuttling electrons toward the respiratory chain.
evidence: The abstract describes results from respirometry experiments.

claim: Transcriptomics studies indicated remodeling of redox metabolism to compensate for a shortage of redox equivalents in the ∆mftG mutant.
source: Transcriptomics studies also indicated remodeling of redox metabolism to compensate for a shortage of redox equivalents.
evidence: The abstract describes findings from transcriptomic analysis.

claim: Environmental mycobacteria like M. smegmatis utilize sugars, polyols, small organic acids, fatty acids, or sterols for their growth.
source: Especially environmental mycobacteria like M. smegmatis utilize for instance sugars, polyols, small organic acids, fatty acids, or sterols for their growth (Tsukamura, 1966).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tsukamura, 1966.

claim: M. tuberculosis is the causative agent of tuberculosis.
source: While obligate pathogens like M. tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis, are more limited in their menu, they still retain the ability to metabolize various nutrients available in the host organism (Bloch and Segal, 1956; Zimmermann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about M. tuberculosis.

claim: M. tuberculosis retains the ability to metabolize various nutrients available in the host organism.
source: While obligate pathogens like M. tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis, are more limited in their menu, they still retain the ability to metabolize various nutrients available in the host organism (Bloch and Segal, 1956; Zimmermann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bloch and Segal, 1956 and Zimmermann et al., 2017.

claim: Alcohols like ethanol are readily consumed by many mycobacterial species.
source: Intriguingly, alcohols like ethanol are readily consumed by many mycobacterial species, but the metabolic pathway for ethanol consumption requires genes related to the biosynthesis of the unusual redox cofactor mycofactocin (MFT; Haft, 2011; Krishnamoorthy et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Haft, 2011 and Krishnamoorthy et al., 2019.

claim: The metabolic pathway for ethanol consumption in mycobacteria requires genes related to the biosynthesis of mycofactocin.
source: Intriguingly, alcohols like ethanol are readily consumed by many mycobacterial species, but the metabolic pathway for ethanol consumption requires genes related to the biosynthesis of the unusual redox cofactor mycofactocin (MFT; Haft, 2011; Krishnamoorthy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haft, 2011 and Krishnamoorthy et al., 2019.

claim: Inactivation of the mycofactocin biosynthetic gene cluster mftA-F showed a severe impact on the growth of M. smegmatis and M. marinum cultivated on ethanol as the sole carbon source.
source: Indeed, the inactivation of the mycofactocin biosynthetic gene cluster mftA-F (Figure 1A) showed a severe impact on the growth of M. smegmatis and M. marinum cultivated on ethanol as the sole carbon source.
evidence: This statement describes experimental results and references Figure 1A.

claim: M. tuberculosis showed a growth deficit on media containing ethanol and cholesterol when mycofactocin biosynthesis was inactivated.
source: For M. tuberculosis, a similar growth deficit on media containing ethanol and cholesterol was observed (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krishnamoorthy et al., 2019.

claim: The gene MSMEG_6242, encoding a MFT-associated alcohol dehydrogenase (termed Mno or Mdo), is strictly required for alcohol utilization in M. smegmatis.
source: In M. smegmatis, it was shown that the gene MSMEG_6242, encoding a MFT-associated alcohol dehydrogenase (termed Mno or Mdo), is strictly required for alcohol utilization.
evidence: This statement describes experimental findings about a specific gene.

claim: Mno/Mdo was demonstrated to catalyze methanol metabolism in M. smegmatis.
source: Mno/Mdo was also demonstrated to catalyze methanol metabolism in the same organism (Dubey et al., 2018) and involvement of mycofactocin in this process was suggested (Dubey and Jain, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dubey et al., 2018.

claim: Involvement of mycofactocin in methanol metabolism was suggested.
source: Mno/Mdo was also demonstrated to catalyze methanol metabolism in the same organism (Dubey et al., 2018) and involvement of mycofactocin in this process was suggested (Dubey and Jain, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dubey and Jain, 2019a.

claim: MFT production in M. smegmatis was significantly increased on ethanol as carbon source in comparison to a control cultivated on glucose.
source: Furthermore, a metabolomics study conducted in our lab revealed that MFT production in M. smegmatis was significantly increased on ethanol as carbon source in comparison to a control cultivated on glucose (Peña-Ortiz et al., 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peña-Ortiz et al., 2020a.

claim: A homolog of Mdo was shown to be essential for MFT-dependent ethylene glycol oxidation in Rhodococcus jostii.
source: Recently, a homolog of Mdo was shown to be essential for MFT-dependent ethylene glycol oxidation in Rhodococcus jostii (Shimizu et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shimizu et al., 2024.

claim: Mycofactocin enables alcohol metabolism by acting as an electron acceptor of alcohol dehydrogenases.
source: All of this evidence supported the hypothesis that mycofactocin enables alcohol metabolism by acting as an electron acceptor of alcohol dehydrogenases (Figure 1B; Haft, 2011; Krishnamoorthy et al., 2019).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to Haft, 2011 and Krishnamoorthy et al., 2019, and references Figure 1B.

claim: The MFT gene locus seems to be de-repressed by long-chain fatty acid-CoA esters in M. smegmatis.
source: Intriguingly, the MFT gene locus seems to be de-repressed by long-chain fatty acid-CoA esters in M. smegmatis, which bind to the repressor MftR (Mendauletova and Latham, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mendauletova and Latham, 2022.

claim: Long-chain fatty acid-CoA esters bind to the repressor MftR.
source: Intriguingly, the MFT gene locus seems to be de-repressed by long-chain fatty acid-CoA esters in M. smegmatis, which bind to the repressor MftR (Mendauletova and Latham, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mendauletova and Latham, 2022.

claim: mftD (Rv0694) was upregulated in the dormant state of M. tuberculosis.
source: Furthermore, a comparison of the proteome of active and dormant cells revealed that mftD (Rv0694) was upregulated in the dormant state, which is associated with the persistence of M. tuberculosis in macrophages (Nikitushkin et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nikitushkin et al., 2022.

claim: The dormant state is associated with the persistence of M. tuberculosis in macrophages.
source: Furthermore, a comparison of the proteome of active and dormant cells revealed that mftD (Rv0694) was upregulated in the dormant state, which is associated with the persistence of M. tuberculosis in macrophages (Nikitushkin et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nikitushkin et al., 2022.

claim: Deletion of mftD in M. tuberculosis resulted in increased growth on glucose containing media.
source: Lastly, a study on the impact of mycofactocin inactivation (∆mftD) on M. tuberculosis showed increased growth on glucose containing media as well as a decreased number of mycobacterial cells in a mouse model after the onset of hypoxia (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krishnamoorthy et al., 2021.

claim: Deletion of mftD in M. tuberculosis resulted in a decreased number of mycobacterial cells in a mouse model after the onset of hypoxia.
source: Lastly, a study on the impact of mycofactocin inactivation (∆mftD) on M. tuberculosis showed increased growth on glucose containing media as well as a decreased number of mycobacterial cells in a mouse model after the onset of hypoxia (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krishnamoorthy et al., 2021.

claim: Mycofactocin is a ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptide (RiPP).
source: Mycofactocin is a ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptide (RiPP; Ayikpoe et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ayikpoe et al., 2019.

claim: The precursor peptide MftA is bound by its chaperone MftB.
source: After translation, the precursor peptide MftA is bound by its chaperone MftB and undergoes several modifications until it matures into a redox-active molecule.
evidence: This describes the biosynthetic pathway of mycofactocin.

claim: The C-terminal core peptide (Val-Tyr) of MftA is decarboxylated and cyclized by the radical S-adenosyl methionine (rSAM) maturase MftC.
source: More precisely, its C-terminal core peptide (Val-Tyr) is decarboxylated and cyclized by the radical S-adenosyl methionine (rSAM) maturase MftC (Khaliullin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Khaliullin et al., 2017.

claim: The cyclized core peptide (AHDP) is liberated from the precursor by the peptidase MftE.
source: The cyclized core peptide (AHDP) is liberated from the precursor by the peptidase MftE (Ayikpoe et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ayikpoe et al., 2018.

claim: The flavoenzyme MftD deaminates AHDP to premycofactocin (PMFT) thus creating a redox-active ketoamide moiety.
source: The flavoenzyme MftD further deaminates AHDP to premycofactocin (PMFT) thus creating a redox-active ketoamide moiety (Ayikpoe and Latham, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ayikpoe and Latham, 2019.

claim: In vivo, mycofactocins exist in oligoglycosylated forms (MFT-n), where n denotes the number of β–1,4-linked glucose moieties.
source: In vivo, mycofactocins exist in oligoglycosylated forms (MFT-n), where n denotes the number of β–1,4-linked glucose moieties.
evidence: This describes the in vivo form of mycofactocin.

claim: The glycosylation of mycofactocin requires the presence of the glycosyltransferase MftF.
source: The glycosylation requires the presence of the glycosyltransferase MftF (Peña-Ortiz et al., 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peña-Ortiz et al., 2020a.

claim: In some mycobacteria, the glycosyl chain of MFT-n is further modified by methylation at the second sugar moiety (yielding MMFT-n) by the mycofactocin-associated methyltransferase MftM.
source: In some mycobacteria, the glycosyl chain of MFT-n is further modified by methylation at the second sugar moiety (yielding MMFT-n) by the mycofactocin-associated methyltransferase MftM (Ellerhorst et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ellerhorst et al., 2022.

claim: The reduction of M/MFT-n to M/MFT-nH2 during growth on ethanol is likely to be catalyzed by the alcohol dehydrogenase Mno/Mdo.
source: The reduction of M/MFT-n to M/MFT-nH2 during growth on ethanol is likely to be catalyzed by the above-mentioned alcohol dehydrogenase Mno/Mdo (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2019; Dubey and Jain, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krishnamoorthy et al., 2019 and Dubey and Jain, 2019a.

claim: It is unclear how MFT-nH2 is re-oxidized to MFT-n after reduction by Mno/Mdo or other enzymes.
source: However, two important questions remained open concerning the mycofactocin system. First, it is unclear how MFT-nH2 is re-oxidized to MFT-n after reduction by Mno/Mdo or other enzymes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: The role of the mftG gene encoding a flavoenzyme of the glucose-methanol-choline (GMC) oxidoreductase superfamily remained unknown.
source: Second, the role of the mftG gene (Figure 1A), the terminal gene in the mft gene cluster of mycobacteria, encoding a flavoenzyme of the glucose-methanol-choline (GMC) oxidoreductase superfamily remained unknown.
evidence: This identifies another knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: GMC oxidoreductases are present in bacteria, fungi, plants, and insects.
source: GMC oxidoreductases are present in bacteria, fungi, plants, and insects (Sützl et al., 2019; Cavener, 1992) and are known to catalyze redox reactions using a variety of different types of substrates and electron acceptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sützl et al., 2019 and Cavener, 1992.

claim: GMC oxidoreductases are known to catalyze redox reactions using a variety of different types of substrates and electron acceptors.
source: GMC oxidoreductases are present in bacteria, fungi, plants, and insects (Sützl et al., 2019; Cavener, 1992) and are known to catalyze redox reactions using a variety of different types of substrates and electron acceptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sützl et al., 2019 and Cavener, 1992.

claim: Fungal glucose oxidases are used in portable glucose biosensors for diabetes patients.
source: Prominent examples are the fungal glucose oxidases, which are used in portable glucose biosensors for diabetes patients (Ferri et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ferri et al., 2011.

claim: Alcohol oxidases from the methylotrophic yeast Pichia pastoris use oxygen as an electron acceptor.
source: Other important representatives are the alcohol oxidases from the methylotrophic yeast Pichia pastoris, which uses oxygen as an electron acceptor (Koch et al., 2016), or the choline dehydrogenase of E. coli, which feeds electrons into the electron transport chain (Landfald and Strøm, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Koch et al., 2016.

claim: The choline dehydrogenase of E. coli feeds electrons into the electron transport chain.
source: Other important representatives are the alcohol oxidases from the methylotrophic yeast Pichia pastoris, which uses oxygen as an electron acceptor (Koch et al., 2016), or the choline dehydrogenase of E. coli, which feeds electrons into the electron transport chain (Landfald and Strøm, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Landfald and Strøm, 1986.

claim: MftG is a protein of the GMC superfamily with an intact FAD binding pocket and a conserved active site histidine.
source: Primary sequence alignments with known members of the GMC family and AlphaFold (Varadi et al., 2022; Jumper et al., 2021) prediction of the tertiary structure of MftG (WP_014877070.1) from M. smegmatis MC2 155 (Figure 2A) confirmed that MftG is a protein of the GMC superfamily with an intact FAD binding pocket and a conserved active site histidine (Aleksenko et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignments and structural predictions, with references to Figure 2A and citations.

claim: A hallmark of the MftG subfamily of GMC oxidoreductases is their tight genetic linkage to the mycofactocin biosynthetic gene cluster mftA-F.
source: While these properties are general characteristics of the GMC superfamily, a hallmark of the MftG subfamily of GMC oxidoreductases is their tight genetic linkage to the mycofactocin biosynthetic gene cluster mftA-F (Haft, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haft, 2011.

claim: MFT-associated GMC homologs are defined by three protein families: TIGR03970.1, TIGR04542, and NF038210.1.
source: These MFT-associated GMC homologs are defined by three protein families. The first, TIGR03970.1 (dehydrogenase, Rv0697 family) describes proteins from various actinobacteria and includes the M. smegmatis homolog. The other two families are TIGR04542 (GMC_mycofac_2) and NF038210.1 (GMC_mycofac_3).
evidence: This describes the classification of MftG homologs based on protein family databases.

claim: TIGR04542 is specific to the Gordonia genus.
source: TIGR04542 is specific to the Gordonia genus, while NF038210.1 is exclusive to the Dietzia genus (Haft, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haft, 2011.

claim: NF038210.1 is exclusive to the Dietzia genus.
source: TIGR04542 is specific to the Gordonia genus, while NF038210.1 is exclusive to the Dietzia genus (Haft, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haft, 2011.

claim: In a total of 312 genomes that contained either mftC or mftG, 311 harbored an mftC homolog, and 235 a putative mftG homolog.
source: In a total of 312 genomes that contained either mftC or mftG, 311 harbored an mftC homolog, and 235 a putative mftG homolog.
evidence: This presents quantitative results from co-occurrence analysis.

claim: In 234 genomes mftC and mftG co-occurred.
source: In 234 genomes the two genes co-occurred (Figure 2C).
evidence: This presents quantitative results from co-occurrence analysis and references Figure 2C.

claim: Only one genome (Herbiconiux sp. L3-i23) encoding a bona fide mftG did not harbor any mftC homolog.
source: Only one genome (Herbiconiux sp. L3-i23) encoding a bona fide mftG did not harbor any mftC homolog.
evidence: This presents a specific exception found in the co-occurrence analysis.

claim: Herbiconiux sp. L3-i23 contains mftD, mftF, and a potential mftA gene but lost mftB, C and E.
source: However, close inspection revealed the presence of mftD, mftF, and a potential mftA gene but a loss of mftB, C and E in this organism.
evidence: This describes the genomic content of a specific organism.

claim: About 25% of the genomes encoding MftC lack an MftG enzyme.
source: On the other hand, about 25% of the genomes encoding MftC lack an MftG enzyme.
evidence: This presents a quantitative finding from the co-occurrence analysis.

claim: Almost no growth of ΔmftG was detected on ethanol.
source: Indeed, almost no growth of ΔmftG was detected on ethanol (Figure 3A), whereas the growth curve of the ∆mftG mutant on glucose-containing media was indistinguishable from the isogenic WT strain (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes experimental results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The growth curve of the ∆mftG mutant on glucose-containing media was indistinguishable from the isogenic WT strain.
source: Indeed, almost no growth of ΔmftG was detected on ethanol (Figure 3A), whereas the growth curve of the ∆mftG mutant on glucose-containing media was indistinguishable from the isogenic WT strain (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes experimental results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: WT and ∆mftG cells displayed significant growth with 5 g L–1 acetate or 10 g L–1 glycerol.
source: Notably, WT and ∆mftG cells displayed significant growth with 5 g L–1 acetate or 10 g L–1 glycerol.
evidence: This describes experimental results from growth assays.

claim: A prolonged lag phase of the ΔmftG strain was detected on 1-propanol (29 h), 1-butanol (18 h), and 1,3-propanediol (20 h) compared to the WT strain.
source: However, evaluation of the growth using other alcohols showed differential behavior. A prolonged lag phase of the ΔmftG strain was detected on 1-propanol (29 h), 1-butanol (18 h), and 1,3-propanediol (20 h) compared to the WT strain.
evidence: This describes experimental results from growth assays on different alcohols.

claim: A putative 1,3-propanediol dehydrogenase (MSMEG_6239) is present in the same operon as MSMEG_6242.
source: Interestingly, a putative 1,3-propanediol dehydrogenase (MSMEG_6239) is present in the same operon as MSMEG_6242, indicating that 1,3-propanediol degradation might be also MFT-dependent (Dubey and Jain, 2019b).
evidence: This describes genomic organization and is supported by a citation to Dubey and Jain, 2019b.

claim: 1,3-propanediol degradation might be also MFT-dependent.
source: Interestingly, a putative 1,3-propanediol dehydrogenase (MSMEG_6239) is present in the same operon as MSMEG_6242, indicating that 1,3-propanediol degradation might be also MFT-dependent (Dubey and Jain, 2019b).
evidence: This is an inference based on genomic organization and is supported by a citation to Dubey and Jain, 2019b.

claim: The ΔmftG mutant showed the ability to grow to a small extent on formic acid in contrast to the WT.
source: While no further defect regarding carbon source utilization was detected, the ΔmftG mutant showed the ability to grow to a small extent on formic acid in contrast to the WT.
evidence: This describes results from phenotype microarray analysis.

claim: The lack of the mftG gene did not induce relevant sensitivity towards antibiotics and stressors compared to WT when grown on glucose alone.
source: Besides the different usage of carbon sources, only minor differences in bacterial growth were found in some of the sensitivity plates (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) demonstrating that the lack of the mftG gene did not induce relevant sensitivity towards antibiotics and stressors compared to WT when grown on glucose alone.
evidence: This describes results from phenotype microarray analysis and references Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Complementation of the ΔmftG deletion resulted in the restoration of growth on 10 g L–1 ethanol.
source: First, the complementation of the ΔmftG deletion using an integrative vector carrying the mftG gene (ΔmftG attB::pMCpAINT-mftG, here named ΔmftG-mftG) was performed and resulted in the restoration of growth on 10 g L–1 ethanol.
evidence: This describes results from genetic complementation experiments.

claim: The complemented strain displayed a shorter lag phase, a faster second exponential growth phase, and a higher final biomass yield compared to the WT.
source: Intriguingly, the growth curve of the complemented strain, which could be dysregulated in mftG expression, displayed a shorter lag phase, a faster second exponential growth phase, and a higher final biomass yield compared to the WT (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes experimental results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Duplication of the mftG gene in the WT strain showed enhanced growth.
source: However, duplication of the mftG gene using the same vector in the WT strain (WT attB::pMCpAINT-mftG, here named WT-mftG) also showed enhanced growth.
evidence: This describes experimental results from gene duplication experiments.

claim: MftG might catalyze a rate-limiting step during ethanol utilization.
source: These results indicate that MftG might catalyze a rate-limiting step during ethanol utilization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enhanced growth observed with mftG overexpression.

claim: Ethanol consumption during exponential growth of WT mycobacteria was accompanied by acetic acid production.
source: As reported previously, ethanol consumption during exponential growth of WT mycobacteria was accompanied by acetic acid production (Figure 3E), a process known as overflow metabolism where the rate of ethanol oxidation to acetate exceeds the rate of carbon assimilation for biomass formation during fast growth (Peña-Ortiz et al., 2020a; Peña-Ortiz et al., 2020b).
evidence: This describes experimental results shown in Figure 3E and is supported by citations.

claim: Overflow metabolism is a process where the rate of ethanol oxidation to acetate exceeds the rate of carbon assimilation for biomass formation during fast growth.
source: As reported previously, ethanol consumption during exponential growth of WT mycobacteria was accompanied by acetic acid production (Figure 3E), a process known as overflow metabolism where the rate of ethanol oxidation to acetate exceeds the rate of carbon assimilation for biomass formation during fast growth (Peña-Ortiz et al., 2020a; Peña-Ortiz et al., 2020b).
evidence: This defines overflow metabolism and is supported by citations to Peña-Ortiz et al., 2020a and 2020b.

claim: The consumption of ethanol and the production of acetic acid remained at a very low level in the ∆mftG strain.
source: Although the ∆mftG strain could achieve residual growth after 45 h, the consumption of ethanol and the production of acetic acid remained at a very low level. (Figure 3C and E).
evidence: This describes experimental results shown in Figures 3C and 3E.

claim: Enzymatic activities supporting ethanol oxidation to acetate are not completely abolished in ∆mftG mutants.
source: While this finding is in line with the occurrence of a metabolic roadblock in the ∆mftG mutant, it indicates, however, that enzymatic activities supporting ethanol oxidation to acetate are not completely abolished in ∆mftG mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of residual ethanol consumption and acetate production.

claim: Simultaneous feeding with ethanol and glucose enhanced the growth yield of the ∆mftG mutant.
source: This interpretation is also supported by growth curves recorded on a combination of ethanol and glucose, where a simultaneous feeding enhanced the growth yield of the ∆mftG mutant (Figure 3D) suggesting at least partially intact ethanol utilization in ∆mftG cells.
evidence: This describes experimental results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: WT and the ΔmftG mutant produced a similar amount of acetaldehyde regardless of whether ethanol was used as the sole carbon source or supplemented.
source: Interestingly, when comparing WT and the ΔmftG mutant, we noticed that both strains produced a similar amount of acetaldehyde regardless of whether ethanol was used as the sole carbon source or supplemented (Figure 3F), indicating that acetaldehyde formation is not altered in the mutant strain.
evidence: This describes experimental results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Acetaldehyde formation is not altered in the ΔmftG mutant strain.
source: Interestingly, when comparing WT and the ΔmftG mutant, we noticed that both strains produced a similar amount of acetaldehyde regardless of whether ethanol was used as the sole carbon source or supplemented (Figure 3F), indicating that acetaldehyde formation is not altered in the mutant strain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the acetaldehyde quantification results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ΔmftG mutants grew well on acetate.
source: At this point, it may be helpful to revisit the fact that ΔmftG mutants grew well on acetate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes experimental results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: mftG is not required for acetaldehyde and acetate assimilation.
source: This observation together with the detection of acetaldehyde and acetate in the supernatants of ΔmftG cultures excludes the hypothesis that mftG is required for acetaldehyde and acetate assimilation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the growth and metabolite data.

claim: The overexpression strains displayed higher rates of ethanol consumption as well as an earlier onset of acetate overflow metabolism and acetate consumption.
source: When investigating the carbon metabolism of the ΔmftG-mftG (complement) and WT-mftG (overexpression) strains, an inverted phenotype became visible. Parallel to the accelerated and enhanced growth described above (Figure 3A), the overexpression strains displayed higher rates of ethanol consumption as well as an earlier onset of acetate overflow metabolism and acetate consumption (Figure 3E).
evidence: This describes experimental results shown in Figures 3A and 3E.

claim: MftG activity is, at least indirectly, related to ethanol oxidation.
source: These results indicate that MftG activity is, at least indirectly, related to ethanol oxidation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolic phenotypes observed.

claim: The accelerated turnover of ethanol to acetate could explain the enhanced final growth yield of the complement and overexpression strains.
source: Notably, the accelerated turnover of the volatile substrate ethanol, which is subject to substantial evaporation during the cultivation process, to acetate, which is less volatile, could explain the enhanced final growth yield of the complement and overexpression strains.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed growth phenotype.

claim: Simultaneous feeding with 10 g L–1 glucose and 10 g L–1 ethanol promoted the growth of the ∆mftG mutant.
source: Surprisingly, simultaneous feeding with 10 g L–1 glucose and 10 g L–1 ethanol even promoted the growth of the ∆mftG mutant.
evidence: This describes experimental results from growth assays.

claim: Bacterial cultures grown on glucose or ethanol as the sole carbon source and under starvation displayed a similar percentage of dead cells after a cultivation period of 72 h, regardless of the genotype.
source: Regardless of the genotype, the bacterial cultures grown on glucose or ethanol as the sole carbon source and under starvation displayed a similar percentage of dead cells after a cultivation period of 72 h.
evidence: This describes experimental results from flow cytometry analysis.

claim: The inability of ∆mftG cells to grow on ethanol alone is not due to ethanol toxicity.
source: We, therefore, conclude that the inability of ∆mftG cells to grow on ethanol alone is not due to ethanol toxicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cell viability data.

claim: Measurements of the transmembrane potential did not reveal any disturbance of the proton motif force (PMF) in the ∆mftG mutant.
source: This conclusion was further supported by measurements of the transmembrane potential that did not reveal any disturbance of the proton motif force (PMF) in the mutant (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes experimental results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: M. smegmatis ∆mftC cells showed no differences in transmembrane potential compared to WT.
source: Previous studies of the transmembrane potential of M. smegmatis ∆mftC cells, another mutant unable to grow on ethanol as a carbon source, showed the same pattern with no differences compared to WT (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krishnamoorthy et al., 2019.

claim: An elevated proportion of dead cells was detected when ∆mftG was cultivated on combined carbon sources, while the WT tolerated this condition well.
